experiments.title: Race Condition in Financial Counter
experiments.subtitle: Non-atomic read-modify-write corrupts transaction counters under concurrent load
experiments.scenario: A fraud detection service tracks per-merchant transaction counts in real time. Each incoming payment request increments a counter for the merchant ID. The service runs as a singleton Spring bean inside a high-throughput API gateway handling 50,000 requests per second. Counters are read every 10 seconds to trigger fraud alerts when thresholds are crossed.
experiments.impact: Under concurrent load, the non-atomic get-then-put sequence allows two threads to read the same stale counter value, both compute an increment, and write back — causing one increment to be silently lost. At peak load, counters can undercount by 10-30%, causing the fraud detection system to miss velocity thresholds and fail to block fraudulent merchants in time.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent structural modifications can corrupt the map or cause infinite loops
UNSAFE: get() reads a value that another thread may already have read and is about to overwrite
UNSAFE: increment computed on a stale value — another thread may have already incremented
UNSAFE: put() overwrites whatever any other thread may have written since the read on line 11

experiments.failureExplanation: HashMap provides no thread-safety guarantees. Two threads executing recordTransaction() concurrently can both read the same value (e.g., 42) on line 11, both compute newValue = 43, and both write 43 back — resulting in a net increment of 1 instead of 2. At high concurrency, this lost-update race can occur thousands of times per second. Concurrent structural changes (resizing) can also corrupt the map itself — on older JDKs even causing infinite loops in get().

assessment.text: Two threads call recordTransaction("merchant-99") simultaneously on a HashMap-backed counter currently at 100. What is the most likely outcome?
options: A) The counter will always reach 102 because Java ensures atomic map updates
B) The counter may end up at 101 due to a lost update race condition
C) A ConcurrentModificationException is always thrown
D) The counter will reach 102 but with a slight delay
assessment.explanation: Both threads read 100 before either writes, then both write 101, leaving the counter at 101 instead of 102. ConcurrentModificationException can occur but only during iteration, not simple get/put. Java makes no atomicity guarantees for HashMap operations.

assessment.text: Which replacement correctly fixes the race condition in recordTransaction()?
options: A) Wrapping the entire method body in a synchronized block on `this`
B) Using ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> with computeIfAbsent + incrementAndGet()
C) Replacing HashMap with a TreeMap
D) Adding the volatile keyword to the counters field
assessment.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap provides thread-safe structural operations, and AtomicLong.incrementAndGet() is a hardware-level atomic CAS — eliminating both map-level and counter-level races. Synchronized works but serializes all merchants through one lock. TreeMap is not thread-safe. volatile only ensures visibility of the reference, not atomicity of the increment.

assessment.text: When should you prefer LongAdder over AtomicLong for a fraud counter?
options: A) When you need the most recent exact value at any instant
B) When many threads hammer the same single merchant counter simultaneously
C) When you have many distinct merchants with low per-merchant concurrency
D) When you need to persist the counter value to a database
assessment.explanation: LongAdder uses cell striping to reduce CAS contention — it shines when many threads contend on the exact same counter. For many distinct merchants with low per-merchant concurrency, AtomicLong is simpler and sufficient. LongAdder.sum() is also not point-in-time consistent, making it unsuitable when exact instantaneous reads are required.

experiments.title: Deadlock in Money Transfer
experiments.subtitle: Inconsistent lock acquisition order between two accounts causes circular wait
experiments.scenario: A core banking service processes money transfers between accounts. Each transfer acquires a lock on the source account and then on the target account before modifying balances. When two transfers run concurrently in opposite directions — Thread 1 transferring from Account A to Account B while Thread 2 transfers from Account B to Account A — each thread locks its source account first, then blocks waiting for the other's target account lock.
experiments.impact: Both threads block indefinitely, holding their locks and preventing all other transfers involving Account A or Account B. In production, this manifests as payment timeouts and customer-visible transaction failures. The deadlock can only be resolved by a timeout or application restart. If multiple account pairs are involved, deadlock can cascade and freeze the entire transfer processing pool.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: always acquires source lock first — ordering depends on caller, not on a canonical key order

Thread 2 calls transfer("B", "A", ...) and acquires lock B, then blocks waiting for lock A. Neither thread can proceed — this is a classic circular wait (the fourth necessary condition for deadlock). Because synchronized blocks do not time out, both threads remain blocked indefinitely.

assessment.text: Why does acquiring locks in account ID order prevent deadlock?
options: A) Because it makes lock acquisition faster by reducing contention
B) Because it eliminates the circular wait condition — all threads acquire locks in the same global order, so no cycle can form
C) Because String.compareTo() is atomic and prevents race conditions
D) Because the JVM guarantees that lexicographically ordered locks are acquired atomically
assessment.explanation: Deadlock requires a circular wait: T1 holds resource A and waits for B, while T2 holds B and waits for A. If all threads always acquire locks in the same global order (e.g., lower ID first), no thread can hold a lock that another thread is waiting for before acquiring the lock the first thread wants — the cycle cannot form.

assessment.explanation: ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() directly queries the JVM's lock management subsystem and returns the thread IDs involved in a deadlock cycle within milliseconds. Polling it every 5-10 seconds on a watchdog thread provides near-real-time deadlock detection. HTTP error rates and logs are lagging indicators that only surface after customers are already impacted.

experiments.title: Livelock in Payment Retry Loop
experiments.subtitle: Two payment processors repeatedly collide and back off simultaneously, making no progress
experiments.scenario: A payment processing cluster runs two processor instances competing to acquire a distributed advisory lock before processing a pending payment batch. When the lock is unavailable, each processor catches the failure, waits a fixed delay, and retries. Because both processors start at nearly the same time and use the same fixed back-off interval, they perpetually retry in lockstep — each waking up to find the other has just reacquired the resource.
experiments.impact: No payment batches are processed despite both processors being fully healthy and runnable. The livelock is invisible to basic health checks (threads are RUNNABLE, not BLOCKED), causing payment settlement delays that compound over time. Without jitter, the problem worsens under higher concurrency as more processors join the collision pattern.

experiments.failureExplanation: Both processor threads call process() at the same time. One acquires the lock; the other catches LockUnavailableException and sleeps 500ms. The first processor finishes quickly and releases the lock. The second processor wakes up, acquires the lock — but by this time the first processor has also looped back and collides again. With a fixed 500ms delay and near-identical processing times, the two processors synchronize their retry cycles and repeatedly deny each other the lock indefinitely.

assessment.text: What is the key difference between a deadlock and a livelock?
options: A) Deadlock always involves more threads than livelock
B) In deadlock, threads are BLOCKED; in livelock, threads are RUNNABLE but make no progress
C) Livelock only occurs in distributed systems while deadlock is JVM-local
D) Deadlock is detected by the JVM; livelock is not
assessment.explanation: In deadlock, threads are BLOCKED waiting for a lock and consume no CPU. In livelock, threads are RUNNABLE — they actively retry, sleep, and retry — but are caught in a pattern where none ever achieves its goal. This makes livelock harder to detect because health checks see active, non-stuck threads.

assessment.text: Why does adding a fixed delay (Thread.sleep(500)) fail to prevent livelock?
options: A) Because Thread.sleep() is not thread-safe
B) Because a fixed delay causes all competing threads to wake up at the same time and collide again
C) Because 500ms is too short a delay for payment processing
D) Because Thread.sleep() does not release held locks
assessment.explanation: If all threads use the same fixed delay and start at nearly the same time, they will sleep for 500ms, wake up together, and collide again on the lock — perpetuating the lockstep cycle. The fix is randomized jitter that desynchronizes wake-up times.

assessment.text: In the full-jitter exponential backoff formula `long cap = BASE * (1L << attempt); long jitter = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, cap + 1)`, what does the `1L << attempt` expression do?
options: A) It divides the base delay by the attempt number to decrease wait time
B) It doubles the maximum delay window on each attempt (2^attempt)
C) It generates a random seed for ThreadLocalRandom
D) It limits the number of retries to the CPU count
assessment.explanation: 1L << attempt is a left bit shift equivalent to 2^attempt. Combined with BASE_DELAY_MS, it creates a cap that doubles on each retry: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms… This exponential growth reduces the retry rate over time, alleviating pressure on the shared resource while jitter prevents synchronized wake-ups.

experiments.title: False Sharing in Payment Throughput
experiments.subtitle: Adjacent volatile fields on the same CPU cache line cause cross-core invalidations and 3-4x throughput loss
experiments.scenario: A high-frequency payment processing engine maintains per-processor success and failure counters in a shared PaymentStats object. Each counter is updated by a separate CPU core. Performance profiling shows the payment throughput is 3x lower than the theoretical hardware limit. CPU performance counters reveal an unusually high rate of L1/L2 cache-line invalidations. The two counters are declared adjacent in the class, placing them on the same 64-byte CPU cache line.
experiments.impact: Every time Core 1 increments successCount, it invalidates the cache line on Core 2 — even though Core 2 only uses failureCount. Core 2 must fetch the cache line from Core 1 (or L3/RAM) before it can write, adding dozens of nanoseconds per update. At 10M+ operations per second, this serializes updates that should be fully parallel, cutting throughput by 60-75%.

experiments.failureExplanation: Modern CPUs transfer memory in 64-byte cache lines. When Core 1 writes successCount and Core 2 writes failureCount, both cores hold the same cache line in MODIFIED state. The MESI protocol forces each write to invalidate the other core's copy, requiring a cache-line bounce through L3 (or main memory) before the next write. This false sharing serializes what should be two fully independent counter updates, reducing throughput by 3-4x. Note that volatile++ is also not atomic — false sharing is a performance bug, but the non-atomic increment is a correctness bug.

assessment.text: Why does writing to `failureCount` on Core 2 impact the performance of writing `successCount` on Core 1, even though they are independent fields?
options: A) Because volatile fields use a global lock that serializes all writes
B) Because both fields fit on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, and a write to one invalidates the other core's copy of the entire line
C) Because Java's memory model requires all volatile writes to be visible to all threads immediately
D) Because the JVM merges consecutive volatile writes into a single operation
assessment.explanation: CPUs exchange memory in 64-byte cache lines. When Core 2 writes failureCount, it must take exclusive ownership of the cache line — invalidating Core 1's cached copy of the same line. Core 1 must then reload the line before its next write to successCount. This cache-line bounce adds ~100ns per operation and serializes logically independent updates.

assessment.text: What JVM flag is required for @Contended to pad fields in application code (outside the JDK)?
options: A) -XX:+UseContendedPadding
B) -XX:-RestrictContended
C) -Djava.util.concurrent.padding=true
D) -XX:ContendedPaddingWidth=128
assessment.explanation: -XX:-RestrictContended removes the restriction that limits @Contended's effect to JDK-internal classes. Without this flag, @Contended annotations in user code are silently ignored and no padding is applied. The default padding width is 128 bytes (two cache lines) to protect against adjacent-line prefetch effects.

assessment.text: In the buggy code, `successCount++` on a volatile long is both a correctness bug and a performance bug. Which statement correctly describes both issues?
options: A) It is correct but slow because volatile flushes the entire CPU cache
B) The ++ is not atomic (read-modify-write race) and the adjacent field causes false sharing — fix both with @Contended + LongAdder
C) It is atomic on x86 but not on ARM; use synchronized for portability
D) volatile++ is atomic only when the JVM is in server mode (-server flag)
assessment.explanation: volatile guarantees visibility (writes are immediately visible to other threads) but not atomicity. The ++ operator compiles to a read, increment, and write — three separate operations that another thread can interleave. This is a correctness bug. Additionally, adjacent volatile fields on the same cache line cause false sharing, the performance bug. @Contended fixes false sharing and LongAdder fixes atomicity.

experiments.title: ABA Problem in a Lock-Free Buffer Pool
experiments.subtitle: A stale CAS succeeds because a reused node came back, so two payments share one buffer
experiments.scenario: A low-latency payment gateway avoids garbage-collection pauses by reusing pre-allocated PaymentBuffer objects. Free buffers sit on a lock-free stack (a Treiber stack): a thread pops a buffer, fills it with a payment instruction, sends it, and pushes the buffer back. pop() reads the top node, reads its next pointer, and uses compareAndSet(top, top.next) to move the head. Under peak load the fraud team finds rare payments whose amount or beneficiary belongs to a different payment.
experiments.impact: If a thread is paused between reading the head and its CAS, other threads can pop that node, use it, and push it back. The head is the same object again, so the stale CAS succeeds and installs an out-of-date next pointer. A buffer that is still in use goes back on the free list, two threads fill the same buffer, and one payment instruction overwrites another — a silent corruption of payment data, not a crash.

experiments.title: Thread Pool Starvation Under Burst Load
experiments.subtitle: Blocking I/O inside a fixed thread pool exhausts all threads, queuing subsequent requests until timeout
experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service uses a fixed thread pool of 10 threads to handle incoming payment requests. Each authorization must call a downstream KYC (Know Your Customer) compliance service over HTTP before returning a result. The KYC service has variable latency (50-500ms). Under normal load, the 10 threads are sufficient. During flash sale events, payment volume spikes and all 10 threads block on KYC HTTP calls simultaneously. New requests queue up, hit their HTTP timeout, and are rejected — even though the payment service CPU usage is near zero.
experiments.impact: During a 30-second burst with 50 concurrent payment requests, all 10 thread pool threads block on KYC calls. The 40 queued requests time out, generating customer-visible payment failures and revenue loss. The service reports 80% error rate despite being entirely healthy — the issue is pool exhaustion from blocking I/O, not any application logic error.

assessment.text: Why does Java 21 virtual threads solve thread pool starvation for I/O-bound workloads?
options: A) Virtual threads use a larger stack size, allowing more I/O operations
B) When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from the carrier thread, freeing the carrier to run other virtual threads
C) Virtual threads run in a separate JVM process and don't share the thread pool
D) Virtual threads make all I/O operations asynchronous automatically
assessment.explanation: Virtual threads (Java 21) are managed by the JVM scheduler. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O (socket read, JDBC query), the JVM 'parks' it and mounts a different virtual thread on the same carrier thread. This means thousands of virtual threads can be active concurrently with only a handful of carrier threads — I/O blocking no longer holds a carrier thread.

assessment.text: Which monitoring signal most reliably indicates thread pool starvation rather than a legitimate traffic spike?

B) CPU utilization near 100%
C) Thread pool active count at maximum while queue size grows and CPU utilization is low
D) High garbage collection pause times
assessment.explanation: Thread pool starvation is characterized by all threads being occupied (active count = max) while CPU utilization is low — the threads are blocked waiting for I/O, not computing. A growing queue confirms incoming requests are waiting for a free thread. High CPU + high error rate would suggest actual overload. Low CPU + max active threads is the starvation signature.

experiments.title: Unsafe Publication of Configuration Object
experiments.subtitle: Without volatile, threads may observe a partially initialized config object due to instruction reordering
experiments.scenario: A payment processing service loads its configuration (rate limits, merchant rules, feature flags) from a database at startup and publishes it to all processing threads via a static field. The configuration is re-loaded periodically to pick up rule changes. Because the static field is not volatile and the configuration object is not immutable, the Java Memory Model permits publishing threads to see instance != null while the internal fields (rules, limits, flags) are still null or zero — a partially initialized object.
experiments.impact: A processing thread reads instance != null and proceeds to call instance.getRules().get(merchantId) — but rules is still null because the JVM reordered the constructor's field assignments after the assignment to instance. This causes NullPointerException in the payment critical path, or silently applies empty rules, allowing payments to bypass fraud checks. The bug is non-reproducible in development (single-core laptops rarely reorder) and only surfaces under heavy multi-core production load.

B) Because the JIT compiler and CPU may reorder the store to instance before the stores to cfg.rules and cfg.rateLimits

D) Because Java always clears object fields to null between constructor calls
assessment.explanation: The Java Memory Model allows the JIT and CPU to reorder independent stores within a thread as long as the single-thread result is preserved. The store to instance and the stores to cfg.rules are independent from the JVM's perspective. Without a happens-before guarantee (from volatile, synchronized, or final fields in constructor), other threads may observe the non-null instance reference before the rules assignment is visible.

assessment.text: How does adding volatile to the instance field fix the unsafe publication?
options: A) volatile prevents the JVM from ever reordering any stores within the JVM
B) A volatile write inserts a memory fence that ensures all preceding writes are visible to any thread that subsequently reads the volatile field
C) volatile makes the entire PaymentConfig object immutable
D) volatile forces the JVM to serialize all accesses to the instance field
assessment.explanation: A volatile write inserts a StoreStore memory barrier before the write and a StoreLoad barrier after, ensuring that all stores that happened before the volatile write (including cfg.rules and cfg.rateLimits assignments) are flushed and visible. Any thread that reads the volatile instance field is guaranteed to see all writes that preceded the volatile store — establishing a happens-before relationship.

assessment.text: Why is this bug more likely to manifest on AWS Graviton (ARM) than on x86 development machines?
options: A) ARM processors are slower and have less memory bandwidth
B) The x86 Total Store Order (TSO) memory model is stronger than ARM's relaxed model — TSO prevents many store reorderings that ARM explicitly allows
C) AWS Graviton uses a different JVM version that has different volatile semantics
D) ARM processors do not support the volatile keyword
assessment.explanation: x86 uses Total Store Order (TSO), which prohibits store-store reordering — coincidentally making many unsafe publications 'work' on x86. ARM uses a weaker memory model that explicitly allows store-store reordering unless memory barriers are inserted. Code that is technically incorrect per the Java Memory Model often appears to work on x86 but fails on ARM, making ARM-based cloud instances (AWS Graviton, Apple M-series) valuable for catching JMM violations. Note that the JIT compiler may still reorder these stores on any CPU, so the code is wrong on x86 too — it just fails less often there.

experiments.scenario: A payment aggregation service chains 20 CompletableFuture steps to fan out balance lookups across 8 downstream ledgers and then merge the results. One step in the chain performs a synchronous JDBC call inside thenApply() to load supplemental account metadata. Under normal load this is invisible, but during month-end batch processing all ForkJoinPool worker threads block waiting on JDBC, completely starving all other CompletableFuture chains in the JVM—including unrelated real-time payment authorizations.
experiments.impact: During month-end reconciliation, the ForkJoinPool common pool (default size = CPU cores - 1) saturates within seconds. Real-time payment authorization latency spikes from 80ms to 45 seconds. Downstream services receive timeout errors. Card-not-present fraud checks are skipped by fallback logic, increasing fraud loss exposure by an estimated $200K per hour of degradation.

When all 7 are blocked on JDBC, every new task submitted to the common pool — from any CompletableFuture chain or parallel stream in the JVM — waits behind them. The pool does not add threads for ordinary blocking calls (it only compensates for ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker), so the starvation spreads across the whole JVM.

B) thenApply() runs the function on the FJP worker that completed the prior stage, blocking it during JDBC I/O, while thenApplyAsync() hands off to the supplied executor so the FJP worker is released immediately

assessment.text: Why does ReentrantLock not pin a virtual thread?
options: A) It uses native OS mutexes that never block

experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service must answer within 2 seconds. options: A) cancel(true) only works after the future has completed
B) For CompletableFuture, the mayInterruptIfRunning flag is ignored: cancel() marks the future as cancelled but never interrupts the thread running the HTTP call
C) cancel(true) closes the connection, but the pool takes 30 seconds to notice
D) supplyAsync() runs the task on the caller's thread, which cannot be cancelled
assessment.explanation: The CompletableFuture Javadoc says mayInterruptIfRunning has no effect, because interrupts are not used to control its processing. assessment.text: In Java 21 Structured Concurrency, which method guarantees that all forked subtasks are cancelled when the scope exits, including on timeout?
options: A) scope.fork(() -> ...).cancel()
B) The try-with-resources block — scope.close() cancels all running forks when the scope exits for any reason
C) StructuredTaskScope automatically sets a 2-second default timeout
D) scope.join() cancels remaining tasks after the first completes
assessment.explanation: StructuredTaskScope is AutoCloseable. When the scope is shut down or closed — after a failure, or when the deadline passes — unfinished subtasks are cancelled by interrupting their threads, and close() waits for them to finish. No subtask outlives the scope, provided the work inside it responds to interruption.

experiments.title: Backpressure Violation in Payment Event Stream
experiments.subtitle: An unbounded buffer between a fast Kafka consumer and a slow consumer ends in OutOfMemoryError and lost events
experiments.scenario: A real-time settlement processor reads a Kafka topic that carries 50,000 settlement events per second during end-of-day settlement. The events are bridged into Reactor with Flux.create(), using the default overflow strategy, and a downstream enrichment step that calls the database handles about 500 events per second. The Kafka consumer auto-commits offsets as soon as records are polled. Nothing in the pipeline tells the consumer to slow down.
experiments.impact: Flux.create()'s default BUFFER strategy is an unbounded in-memory queue, so it grows by about 49,500 events every second. Within minutes the heap is full, the pod dies with OutOfMemoryError, and Kubernetes restarts it. Because the offsets of those buffered events were already auto-committed, Kafka considers them processed: every event that was sitting in the buffer is lost. Settlements are missing until reconciliation finds them the next day, and regulatory settlement reports are wrong.

Because offsets were committed on poll (auto-commit), the events that were only in memory are lost when the process dies. The fix is a demand-driven source: poll Kafka only as fast as the pipeline processes, and commit an offset only after its event has been processed.

options: A) It limits the total number of elements the Flux will emit over its lifetime

C) It throttles the subscriber to process at most n events per second
D) It limits the number of concurrent flatMap inner subscriptions to n
assessment.explanation: limitRate(n) shapes demand: it requests n items and replenishes when 75% have been consumed. That only controls sources that honour requests. assessment.text: For payment settlement events where loss is unacceptable, which design is correct?
options: A) Flux.create() with OverflowStrategy.LATEST so memory stays small
B) Flux.create() with OverflowStrategy.DROP, which discards incoming events when downstream is busy
C) A demand-driven KafkaReceiver with offsets acknowledged only after processing, plus idempotent processing
D) Flux.create() with OverflowStrategy.IGNORE for maximum throughput
assessment.explanation: LATEST and DROP discard events by design, and IGNORE disables backpressure handling entirely. For settlement data the backlog must stay in Kafka: poll only on demand, commit only after processing, and make processing idempotent so redelivery after a failure is safe.

experiments.title: Structured Concurrency Partial Failure Not Propagated
experiments.subtitle: Why StructuredTaskScope.join() without ShutdownOnFailure approves partial payment authorizations
experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service uses Java 21 Structured Concurrency to run three compliance checks in parallel: fraud scoring, KYC (Know Your Customer) verification, and credit limit validation. The team uses a plain StructuredTaskScope to fork all three tasks and joins them before assembling the authorization result. During testing, the KYC service throws a ServiceUnavailableException. The scope.join() returns normally. The code then calls kyc.get() which throws, but the caller catches it as a generic exception and logs it — the payment is approved based on only fraud and limit checks. A KYC-failing customer receives authorization.
experiments.impact: During a 4-hour KYC service outage, 2,340 payment authorizations are approved without KYC verification. Post-incident analysis reveals 18 of those customers are on watchlists. The firm faces regulatory enforcement action under AML (Anti-Money Laundering) regulations, with potential fines of €1M–€10M and mandatory external audit. The incident is classified as a Tier-1 compliance failure.

One of them should be rejected, but both succeed — $1,100 is paid out — and because the second write overwrites the first, the balance ends at $700. assessment.text: Why does PostgreSQL MVCC allow two concurrent transactions to both read the same balance without one blocking the other?
options: A) PostgreSQL uses table-level locks by default for all SELECT statements
B) Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of committed data taken at transaction start, so plain SELECTs do not block
C) The READ COMMITTED isolation level causes each transaction to wait for the other to finish
D) MVCC only applies to INSERT and DELETE, not UPDATE
assessment.explanation: MVCC gives every transaction a consistent snapshot of the database as of its start time (or statement start under READ COMMITTED). Plain SELECTs never block concurrent writers — they simply read the latest committed version visible to their snapshot. This is why two transactions can both read $1,000 and both pass the balance check before either commits.

assessment.text: What is the minimum change needed to prevent the lost-update race in the withdrawal service?

D) Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for the read phase

assessment.text: When should you prefer optimistic locking (@Version) over pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) for balance updates?

B) When conflicting updates are rare and the cost of an occasional retry is acceptable
C) When the database does not support row-level locking
D) When you want to prevent dirty reads under READ UNCOMMITTED isolation
assessment.explanation: Optimistic locking avoids holding a lock during the transaction, which is beneficial when conflicts are infrequent. Under high contention, the retry storm caused by frequent ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureExceptions can degrade throughput more than the queuing cost of a row-level lock.

All four hold, so it is a true deadlock.

D) It disables the connection pool for the audit service entirely
assessment.explanation: AFTER_COMMIT phase means the event handler is invoked only after the publishing transaction has successfully committed — which also means the connection has been returned to the pool. assessment.text: Why does Kafka's at-least-once delivery guarantee make compensation handlers non-idempotent by default?
options: A) Kafka encrypts messages differently on each delivery, causing handlers to compute different results

B) At-least-once delivery means the same message can be delivered more than once (after rebalance, restart, or timeout), so a handler that mutates state unconditionally will apply the mutation multiple times
C) Kafka partitions guarantee ordering but not exactly-once semantics only for producers, not consumers
D) Compensation handlers are always called twice by the saga orchestrator as a redundancy mechanism
assessment.explanation: At-least-once delivery is a Kafka consumer contract: messages are guaranteed to be delivered at least once but may be delivered more times due to consumer rebalances, offset commit failures, or producer retries. A handler that applies a balance credit unconditionally will credit the account once per delivery — making idempotency a mandatory design requirement for any state-mutating handler.

assessment.text: Why must the saga_compensations record be inserted in the same transaction as the balance update rather than in a separate transaction after?
options: A) Separate transactions would cause a foreign key violation on the accounts table
B) If the application crashes between the balance update commit and the compensation record insert, the guard will never be written, allowing a future redelivery to apply a second credit
C) Separate transactions are not supported when using @KafkaListener
D) The saga_compensations insert would deadlock with the accounts update if run sequentially
assessment.explanation: Atomicity is essential: if the balance UPDATE commits but the compensation INSERT does not (due to a crash, network partition, or rollback), a subsequent redelivery finds no guard record and applies a duplicate credit. Writing both changes in a single transaction guarantees that either both succeed or both fail, preserving the idempotency invariant.

assessment.text: What additional database constraint provides a last-resort safety net for the saga_compensations idempotency guard even if two threads race past the exists check simultaneously?

C) A NOT NULL constraint on the saga_id column
D) A FOREIGN KEY constraint linking saga_compensations to the payments table
assessment.explanation: Even with an application-level exists check, two concurrent deliveries can both read false before either insert commits — the same check-then-act race as fin-02. A UNIQUE constraint on (saga_id, step) makes the INSERT atomic, so only one thread can succeed; the second receives a constraint violation and can safely return without applying a second credit.

B) The database transaction and the Kafka produce operation are separate resources with no shared transaction coordinator; a @Transactional Spring context only manages JDBC transactions by default, leaving Kafka outside its scope

assessment.text: What is the core guarantee that the Transactional Outbox pattern provides, and how does it achieve it?

B) Atomic write of the domain record and the event record in a single ACID database transaction, ensuring the event is never lost even if Kafka is unavailable at write time
C) Synchronous Kafka delivery within the same HTTP request lifecycle as the database write
D) Automatic rollback of the database transaction if the Kafka broker rejects the event
assessment.explanation: The outbox pattern leverages the database's own ACID guarantees: writing both the payment and the outbox_event in a single transaction means either both are committed or neither is. The event cannot be lost because it is durably stored in the database; the CDC relay (Debezium) publishes it to Kafka independently with its own retry logic.

assessment.text: How does Debezium read the outbox table without additional polling queries, and what database feature does it rely on?
options: A) Debezium issues a SELECT * FROM outbox_events WHERE processed = false every second using a scheduled job
B) Debezium uses PostgreSQL logical replication (the Write-Ahead Log) to stream row changes in real time, with no polling queries and sub-second latency
C) Debezium registers a PostgreSQL trigger on outbox_events that calls a Kafka producer stored procedure
D) Debezium subscribes to Spring application events published by the outbox repository
assessment.explanation: Debezium acts as a PostgreSQL logical replication consumer, reading the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) stream. Every committed INSERT to outbox_events appears in the WAL and is relayed to Kafka by Debezium — with no polling latency, no additional database load from SELECT queries, and built-in backpressure and retry.

assessment.text: What causes a cache stampede in a Redis-backed balance service?
options: A) Redis running out of memory and evicting keys under LRU policy
B) Multiple threads simultaneously reading a key that just expired, all missing the cache and issuing redundant database queries
C) The database returning different values to different threads due to read isolation
D) Redis replication lag causing primary and replica to return different values
assessment.explanation: A cache stampede occurs when a TTL expiry causes every concurrent thread to see a cache miss at the same instant. Without coordination, all threads independently query the database and attempt to repopulate the cache, overwhelming the database and defeating the caching strategy.

assessment.text: What is the purpose of the double-checked read (re-reading the cache inside the lock) in the Redisson single-flight pattern?
options: A) To verify that the Redisson lock was acquired correctly
B) To ensure the balance returned is always the most recent value from the database
C) To avoid a database query if another thread already populated the cache while the current thread was waiting for the lock
D) To prevent Redis from accepting stale writes from other pods
assessment.explanation: Threads that were queued waiting for the lock check the cache again after acquiring it. The first thread to acquire the lock will find the cache empty and query the database. All subsequent threads will find the cache already populated by the first thread and return immediately without hitting the database.

assessment.text: How does adding TTL jitter (e.g., 55–65 seconds instead of a fixed 60 seconds) reduce cache stampede risk?
options: A) It increases the total time data stays in cache, reducing miss frequency
B) It staggers expiry times across different cache keys and pod write times, so not all keys expire simultaneously
C) It instructs Redis to automatically refresh keys before they expire
D) It prevents any two threads from writing to the same Redis key within the jitter window
assessment.explanation: Jitter spreads expiry events over a time window. When many keys are written at the same moment (a deploy, a warm-up job, a cache flush) with exactly TTL=60s, they all expire together and hit the database at once. With jitter they expire at slightly different times, so the load is spread out. For a single hot key, jitter changes nothing — that case needs the single-flight lock.

assessment.text: What is Redisson's watchdog, and what problem does it solve?
options: A) A monitoring thread that alerts on Redis connection failures
B) A background daemon that periodically renews a lock's TTL while the holder JVM is alive, preventing auto-expiry during long operations
C) A circuit breaker that prevents new lock acquisitions when Redis is overloaded
D) A fallback that acquires a local JVM lock when Redis is unavailable
assessment.explanation: Redisson's watchdog is an internal scheduled task that calls PEXPIRE on a lock key every lockWatchdogTimeout/3 milliseconds, resetting the TTL and preventing auto-expiry. It activates only when lock.lock() is called without an explicit leaseTime, and it stops when lock.unlock() is called or the JVM process terminates.

assessment.text: Why does specifying an explicit leaseTime in lock.lock(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) disable the Redisson watchdog?
options: A) Redisson cannot run the watchdog and a TTL simultaneously due to a Redis limitation
B) An explicit leaseTime signals that the caller has intentionally set a maximum lock duration, so Redisson respects that boundary and disables automatic renewal
C) The watchdog requires a Redisson cluster configuration; it does not work with single-node Redis
D) Explicit TTL locks are stored in a separate Redis keyspace where the watchdog has no access
assessment.explanation: Redisson interprets an explicit leaseTime as a deliberate upper bound set by the application. If the caller specifies leaseTime, Redisson assumes they want the lock to expire at that time regardless of operation status and disables watchdog renewal. Omitting leaseTime (-1 internally) enables watchdog mode.

assessment.text: If a JVM hosting a Redisson watchdog lock crashes mid-operation, how does the lock eventually become available?
options: A) The lock is permanently orphaned and must be manually deleted from Redis
B) Redisson on another pod detects the crash and releases the lock within 1 second
C) The watchdog stops renewing the TTL when the JVM dies, so Redis auto-expires the key after the last-renewed TTL (default up to 30 seconds)
D) The lock is released immediately because Redis monitors JVM process health
assessment.explanation: The watchdog runs inside the holder's JVM. When the JVM crashes, the watchdog thread stops and can no longer renew the lock TTL. Redis then auto-expires the key after the last renewed TTL elapses (up to lockWatchdogTimeout, default 30 seconds), after which another node can acquire the lock. This is safer than a permanent orphan but means retries must wait up to 30 seconds after a crash.

assessment.text: Why does Debezium deliver the same CDC event more than once after a connector restart?
options: A) Debezium uses exactly-once delivery by default; duplicates indicate a misconfiguration
B) Debezium is at-least-once — it saves its source position (LSN) only periodically, and after a restart it republishes every event sent after the last saved position
C) The PostgreSQL WAL deletes events after delivery, so Debezium must re-read from the beginning of the log
D) Debezium deduplicates events using the transaction ID, so duplicates are impossible
assessment.explanation: Debezium is an at-least-once system. It stores its source position (the LSN) in Kafka Connect's offset storage every few seconds. Events sent after the last stored position are published again after a restart. Consumers must be idempotent to handle this.

assessment.text: What SQL pattern makes a reconciliation INSERT idempotent against CDC event redelivery?
options: A) INSERT IGNORE INTO reconciliation_events ...
B) INSERT INTO reconciliation_events ... ON CONFLICT (tx_id, event_type) DO NOTHING
C) MERGE INTO reconciliation_events WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount=amount
D) INSERT INTO reconciliation_events ... IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reconciliation_events WHERE tx_id=?)
assessment.explanation: PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING clause combined with a unique index on (tx_id, event_type) makes the INSERT atomic and idempotent: if a row with the same key already exists, the statement completes successfully with zero rows inserted rather than raising a duplicate-key error. The rowcount return value lets the application decide whether to update dependent aggregates.

assessment.text: What is the key advantage of the Outbox Pattern over relying solely on CDC idempotency for financial reconciliation?
options: A) The outbox pattern eliminates the need for a Kafka broker entirely
B) Each business event is written once, atomically with the business transaction, and carries a stable event_id — so consumers deduplicate on one simple key
C) The outbox pattern uses batch inserts, which are faster than individual CDC events
D) The outbox pattern automatically retries failed events without consumer intervention
assessment.explanation: With the outbox pattern the outbox row is inserted in the same database transaction as the business operation, so each business event produces exactly one row with a unique event_id. Debezium still delivers each row at least once, but deduplicating on event_id is trivial and reliable. Without an outbox, the consumer must build a dedup key from raw table changes, which is harder to get right.

assessment.text: What is the real danger of running INCR and then EXPIRE as two separate commands?
options: A) Concurrent INCR calls can return the same count, so too many requests are allowed
B) If anything stops the EXPIRE after INCR created the key (crash, deploy, timeout), the key has no TTL, never resets, and the merchant is blocked forever
C) EXPIRE resets the counter to 0, so the limit is evaluated incorrectly
D) Redis rejects EXPIRE on keys created by INCR
assessment.explanation: INCR is atomic, so counts are always distinct and the limit is counted correctly. The risk is the gap between the two requests: if EXPIRE never runs after the INCR that returned 1, no later request will set it (they all see counts above 1). The key lives forever, and the merchant is rejected once it reaches the limit.

assessment.text: How does executing INCR and EXPIRE inside a Redis Lua script guarantee atomicity?
options: A) Lua scripts run in a separate Redis thread with higher priority than regular commands
B) Redis executes Lua scripts in its single-threaded event loop without preemption — no other command can run between any two operations within the script
C) Lua scripts lock the entire Redis instance for 100ms, preventing concurrent access
D) Redis replicates Lua scripts before execution, making them durable and atomic
assessment.explanation: Redis runs a Lua script to completion before it processes any other command, and the script runs entirely on the server. So no other client can run a command between the INCR and the EXPIRE, and a client crash cannot stop the script halfway — both commands happen as one unit.

assessment.text: What is a key operational difference between a fixed-window rate limiter (INCR + EXPIRE) and a token bucket (Bucket4j)?
options: A) Token buckets support higher throughput because they do not use Redis

B) Fixed-window limiters reset the count at exact window boundaries, allowing a burst of 2× the limit across the boundary; token buckets smooth traffic with continuous refill, limiting true burst capacity
C) Token buckets count requests in reverse, decrementing from the limit to zero
D) Fixed-window limiters use Lua scripts while token buckets use transactions
assessment.explanation: A fixed-window limiter with a 1-minute window allows up to 100 requests in the last second of minute N and 100 more in the first second of minute N+1 — a 200-request burst in 2 seconds. A token bucket refills at a steady rate (e.g., 100/60 tokens per second) and limits instantaneous burst capacity, making it more suitable for protecting downstream services from sudden spikes.
